```{python}
#| echo: false
from pbc.authoring import excerpt, lesson_header, reproduce_this, source_link
from pbc.mechanics import resonance
from pbc.mechanics.experiments import verifying_scientific_code as experiment
from pbc.verification import checks, driven, estimates, faulty_driven

result = experiment.run()
```

A simulation that runs and prints a smooth curve has shown nothing. The
earlier lessons of this course built their integrators carefully, and each
was compared with an exact solution, but a reader who is given a stepper
written by someone else, or by a program, has no such history. The question
is how to find out whether it is right, and what "right" is allowed to mean.

The answer is a set of tests that do not trust the code they test. Each
compares the result with something the code did not compute: the motion with
no force, the exact oscillator, a quantity the physics conserves. This lesson
runs five such tests on the steppers of the course, and then on six steppers
that are wrong on purpose, each with one fault of the kind that is made in
practice: a missing factor, a sign, a clock that does not run, a state that
leaks from one step to the next. Every fault is caught by a test with a name,
and the tests that miss a fault are as instructive as the one that finds it.

The tests, their order, and the evidence a verifier reports are written down
as the *Scientific validation contract*, in the file
`docs/validation-contract.md` of the repository. The lesson follows the
contract and names it where it applies; the multi-agent review of a later
lesson and the rubric for code written by an agent use the same contract.

The second half of the page takes the contract to where it is needed most.
A model the tests were not written for, the damped driven oscillator, is
turned into code from a written specification and checked, and then the same
specification is handed to a coding agent, whose output is checked and
reviewed in the same way.

## Assumptions

The tests and the program rest on these assumptions. Each one names what
goes wrong when it does not hold.

1. **A claim exists.** The tests check what a method says about itself: its
   order of accuracy and whether it keeps the energy bounded. Code with no
   claim has nothing to check against, and a claim written after seeing the
   results is a description, not a test.
2. **The oscillator is a fair reference.** It has an exact solution, so
   every error is the stepper's. It is also a linear system with a force that
   does not depend on the velocity, so a fault that only matters for a
   nonlinear or velocity-dependent force can pass every test here; the
   contract says what to add for a new model.
3. **The tolerances are fixed first.** They are constants of the module,
   chosen from what a correct method does, before any faulty one is run. A
   tolerance widened until a test passes makes the test measure nothing, as
   the first exercise shows.
4. **Faults are single.** Each faulty stepper has one fault. Real faults
   come in groups and hide each other; the tests do not become less useful
   for it, but the pattern of failures becomes harder to read.
5. **Round-off is below the tolerances.** The exact tests allow $10^{-12}$,
   several orders above the round-off of the numbers used. A method with
   large intermediate values would need its own tolerance.

## What a test may compare with {#explanation}

A test of a simulation has three parts: a claim, a reference, and a
tolerance. The reference decides whether the test is worth anything. If the
reference is computed by the code under test, or by code written from the same
mistaken derivation, the two agree whatever the mistake. A reference is
independent when it comes from somewhere the code did not: an exact solution,
a limiting case, a law, or the experiment's own bookkeeping.

The contract orders five tests, from the cheapest and most basic to the ones
that need a reference solution and a long run. They are the names the rest of
the page uses.

1. **`clock`.** A step of length $\Delta t$ advances the time by $\Delta t$.
   The reference is the step the experiment asked for.
2. **`purity`.** A step depends only on its arguments. The same state, taken
   again after other steps, gives the same result.
3. **`limits`.** Cases with a closed form. With no force the motion is
   uniform, $x = x_0 + v_0 t$; under a constant force $a$ the velocity is
   $v_0 + a t$ exactly, for every method of the course, because the velocity
   update of each is exact for a constant acceleration, and the position is
   $x_0 + v_0 t + \tfrac12 a t^2$, exactly for a method of order 2 or more.
   A method of order 1 may be off by $\tfrac12 a\,\Delta t^2$ in each step,
   and only the excess over that allowance counts.
4. **`convergence-order`.** Halving the step divides the error by $2^p$ for a
   method of order $p$. The reference is the exact oscillator of the earlier
   lessons, and the number is the slope of the error against the step on
   logarithmic axes.
5. **`bounded-energy`.** For a method that claims a bounded energy, the
   energy of the oscillator stays within a band that does not grow. A single
   number cannot tell a band from a trend, so the test compares the width of
   the band in the first periods of a long run with its width in the last.

The first three need no reference solution at all, which is why they come
first: they cost little, and a method that fails them has a fault that the
later results cannot be trusted to show. The last two are the ones that find a
fault which changes the numbers only slightly.

No test proves a method right. Each asks one question that a right method
answers one way. The contract says what a report must therefore contain:
for each test the claim, the measured value, the tolerance, and the verdict,
and a statement of what was not covered. A faulty method is caught when some
test fails; a method that passes has passed those tests, on this model, at
these steps, and no more.

### Six faulty steppers

Each stepper below is wrong on purpose, in one way. They live in
`pbc.verification.faulty`, a module that says so in its first line and that
nothing which simulates may import. Each entry records which correct method it
poses as, so that it is held to that method's claim, and which tests must
catch it. Three of them:

```{python}
#| echo: false
from pbc.verification import faulty

excerpt(faulty.verlet_without_the_half)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
excerpt(faulty.verlet_with_a_stopped_clock)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
excerpt(faulty.verlet_that_remembers_the_acceleration)
```

The six run the same tests as the correct methods, under the claim of the
method they pose as:

```{python}
#| echo: false
excerpt(experiment.gallery)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
print(result.output("gallery"), end="")
```

Each fault fails the tests the gallery names for it and no others, and no
correct method fails any test: the same tests separate the two groups. The
pattern matters more than the count.

- *Verlet without the half* has the wrong coefficient on a term that is of
  second order in the step. Everything it computes is plausible and the
  energy stays in its band. The order is wrong, which the convergence test
  sees, and so is the position under a constant force, which the limit test
  sees without a reference solution of the oscillator.
- *Symplectic Euler with the wrong sign* runs the velocity the wrong way.
  Three tests fail: it is the fault any test would find, and the limit test
  finds it first, with no reference solution and a run of twenty steps.
- *Verlet with a stopped clock* is exact in every physical test, because the
  oscillator does not depend on time. Only the interface test, `clock`, finds
  it, and it would corrupt every simulation with a time-dependent force.
- *Runge-Kutta 4 with equal weights* is of order 2, not 4: accurate enough to
  look like a good method, until the fitted order is compared with the claim.
- *Explicit Euler as symplectic* is a first-order method, as claimed, so the
  convergence test passes. Only the energy test sees that the updates are in
  the wrong order. A test of order alone would have approved it.
- *Verlet that remembers* is exact when its steps are taken one after
  another, which is how every simulation takes them, so every test that only
  runs a simulation passes. Only `purity`, which asks for the same step again
  after others, finds the leaked state.

### A test that cannot fail

A test that passes everything is not evidence. The first protection is the
gallery: every test has a faulty stepper it must fail. The second is to claim
the wrong thing about a correct method. Velocity Verlet claimed to be of order
1 or of order 4 must fail the convergence test, and the true claim must pass:

```{python}
#| echo: false
excerpt(experiment.claimed_orders)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
print(result.output("claimed-orders"), end="")
```

Only the true claim passes. A tolerance is part of the claim; how loose it may
be is the subject of the first exercise.

### An evaluation of a piece of code against the contract

Given a stepper and a claim, the evaluation is the table of findings, a
verdict, and a sentence on what was covered. For a stepper someone else wrote,

report is generated from the findings and nothing is judged by eye:

## From a model to tested code {#model-to-code}

The second exercise below ends on a warning: the linear oscillator cannot
show a fault that needs a force depending on the velocity or on the time.
Every test so far ran on a model chosen because it is easy. The models worth
simulating are not, and their code is written by someone, or something,
other than the person who has to trust it. So take a model with both kinds
of force, write down what its code must do before any code exists, and find
out which of the five tests carry over.

### The model and its specification

A mass $m$ on a spring of constant $k$ moves against a linear drag $b$ and
is pushed by a force that oscillates with the angular frequency $\Omega$:

$$
m\,\ddot x + b\,\dot x + k\,x = F_0 \cos(\Omega t).
$$

The drag depends on the velocity and the driving force on the time. The
lesson *Resonance and driven oscillators* studies what this system does;
here it is only the subject of the tests, and all that is needed from that
lesson is that the motion has a closed form: after a decaying start the mass
swings at the driving frequency with a known amplitude.

The specification of the code has five parts, in the form the coding-agent
workflow of this project gives to every such task
(`docs/coding-agent-workflow.md` in the repository).

- **Physics.** The equation above.
- **Assumptions.** Motion along one line; constant $m$, $k$, $b$, $F_0$,
  and $\Omega$; drag linear in the velocity and against it; the time in the
  cosine is the time of the state, not the time since the first step.
- **Interface.** One function,
  `simulate_driven(initial, mass, k, b, force, omega, dt, n_steps)`, that
  returns the initial state and the state after every step, and refuses a
  mass, a spring constant, or a time step that is not positive and a drag
  that is negative.
- **Units.** SI: kg, N/m, kg/s, N, rad/s, s. The frequency is an angular
  frequency. This line is not a formality: five parameters carry five
  different units, and two of the faults below are unit mistakes.
- **The tests the result must pass.** Four checks of the contract, under
  the claim that the method is of order four.

The physics becomes code term by term. The driving force is a function of
the time, like every force of this course:

```{python}
#| echo: false
excerpt(resonance.driving_force)
```

and the simulation adds it to the spring and the drag, divides by the mass,
and steps with the classical Runge-Kutta method:

```{python}
#| echo: false
excerpt(resonance.simulate_driven)
```

This function is the reference solution. The course has used the same
computation since the resonance lesson; here it is the subject under test.

### Which of the five tests carry over?

`clock` and `purity` test a stepper and stay as they are. `limits` and
`convergence-order` keep their names and get references of this model.
`bounded-energy` has no meaning here: the drag removes energy and the drive
supplies it, so nothing is conserved.

Before adding anything, try what already exists. Two of the six faulty
steppers passed every physical test on the oscillator: the stopped clock,
caught only by `clock`, and the stepper that remembers, caught only by
`purity`. Put each inside the simulation of the driven oscillator, claim
order two as for velocity Verlet, and run the model's checks, which the next
section describes. The force now depends on the time. Decide, before you
look, which of the two faults becomes visible in the motion.

```{python}
#| echo: false
excerpt(experiment.steppers_on_the_model, lines=(6, 13))
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
result.table("steppers-on-the-model")
```

The stopped clock is no longer an interface fault that happens to be
harmless. Its force is evaluated at the same instant for ever, the motion is
wrong, and two checks say so. The stepper that remembers still passes: each
simulation takes its steps one after another on a stepper of its own, which
is the one way of calling it that hides the leak. The model's checks did not
make `purity` unnecessary.

### The four checks of the model

1. **`limits`.** Three cases with a closed form. At rest with no force the
   mass stays at rest. Under a constant force, $\Omega = 0$, it stays at
   the static deflection $F_0/k$. Both hold exactly for any method, because
   the acceleration is zero. With no driving force the motion is the free
   decay, known in closed form, and the simulation must follow it within a
   tolerance fixed for a method of order two or more.
2. **`convergence-order`.** Against the exact driven motion, halving the
   step divides the error by two to the claimed order.
3. **`units`.** New. Write the same experiment in grams, then in
   centimetres, then in milliseconds, converting every number by the power
   of the unit it carries, and convert the result back. The motion must be
   the same. A term with the wrong unit changes when the unit does.
4. **`energy-balance`.** New, and in the place of `bounded-energy`. The
   energy is not conserved, but its change is accounted for:
   $$
   \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\Bigl(\tfrac12 m v^2 + \tfrac12 k x^2\Bigr)
   = F_0 \cos(\Omega t)\,v - b\,v^2 .
   $$
   The left side follows from multiplying the equation of motion by $v$.
   Integrated over the run, the change of the energy must equal the work of
   the drive minus what the drag dissipated. The check computes both
   integrals from the simulated motion and needs no exact solution, which
   is what remains when a model has none.

The unit check is the least familiar, so here is the whole of its
measurement. Each line of the converted call multiplies a number by the
factors its unit holds: a spring constant in N/m is a mass over a time
squared.

```{python}
#| echo: false
excerpt(driven.rescaled, lines=(8, 23))
```

The energy balance is the equation above, term for term:

```{python}
#| echo: false
excerpt(driven.energy_balance)
```

A claim of order one is refused by these checks. The tolerances of the free
decay and of the balance were fixed for a method of order two or more, and
a first-order method measured against them would fail for being what it
says it is. A tolerance belongs to a claim.

### Four faulty simulations

As with the steppers, the checks are worth what they catch. Four
simulations, each the reference solution with one mistake of the kind made
when a model becomes code. Two of them:

```{python}
#| echo: false
excerpt(faulty_driven.drive_not_divided_by_mass)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
excerpt(faulty_driven.drive_frozen_within_the_step)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
result.table("faulty-simulations")
```

Each fault fails a check, and the reference solution fails none. The
patterns can be read like those of the steppers.

- *Drive frozen within the step* is correct in every limit and under every
  change of units. The method has four stages and the force is computed for
  the first. Only the checks that measure accuracy see it: the order is one,
  and the balance does not close. A reader of the code would look at this
  line and see a force at a time.
- *Frequency in hertz* is the unit mistake that the unit check cannot find.
  A factor of $2\pi$ has no unit, so the motion converts correctly from
  grams to kilograms. It is found because the specification said "angular
  frequency" and the exact motion was computed for one.
- *Drag with the wrong sign* fails the first limit that has a drag in it:
  the free motion grows.
- *Drive not divided by the mass* fails everything here. That it does is
  owed to a decision made before any code was run.

### A fault that hides at a convenient value

The mass of the checks is half a kilogram. Suppose it had been one kilogram,
the value a test is most likely to be written with.

```{python}
#| echo: false
result.table("unit-mass")
```

At a mass of one kilogram the missing division changes nothing, and the
simulation converges to the exact motion at fourth order: a wrong program
that passes its sharpest test. The unit check finds it at any mass, and it
names the unit: the motion changes with the unit of mass and with no other,
which says where in the code to look. The parameters of the checks are
deliberately not round numbers, and a test asserts that none of them is one.

## Code a coding agent wrote {#coding-agent}

The specification above was written for a reader who does not share your
history with the code. A coding agent is such a reader: a program that
takes a task in words, writes files, and runs commands. The kind of evidence
in this section has to be stated first, because it is of two kinds. What the
build runs is the reference solution, the checks, and the faulty
simulations: results of this page, computed again with every build. What an
agent did is a record of one session, shown once below and marked "not
verified". This site never runs a coding agent, in its build or in its
checks, and holds no credential of one.

Everything needed to check an agent's work already exists. The claim came
with the task. The checks are the four above. What is new is that the
author of the code will run commands on your machine, and that the code
arrives with a confident summary. The first calls for a sandbox, the second
for a rubric.

### The sandbox profile

The profile is the same for every coding-agent exercise of this project.
Set it up before the agent starts; each rule names what it prevents.

1. **A scratch checkout.** The agent works in a fresh clone or an empty
   directory, never in a checkout you care about. A wrong command then
   costs a directory you can delete.
2. **An allowlist of commands.** The agent may run the tests, the
   formatter, and the task's own scripts, and nothing else: no installer,
   no version control, no shell beyond those commands. Most agents can be
   configured to ask before any other command; refuse. Without a container
   or a separate machine this is a setting of the agent, not a limit your
   machine enforces.
3. **No network beyond the agent's own provider.** The task needs none. An
   agent that fetches a package or a page has left the specification. Like
   the allowlist, this holds only where a container, a firewall, or a
   separate machine enforces it.
4. **The credential stays in your environment.** The agent's account and
   key are yours, kept where its own documentation says, never in a file of
   the checkout and never in a prompt. The agent's commands run as you, so
   every credential in your environment variables is readable to them, not
   only the agent's own key: start the agent in a shell that holds no other.
5. **A budget, set before the start.** A number of steps or tool calls, a
   time, and a cost. When it is spent the session ends, passed or not. This
   is the stopping condition of the lesson on experiment specifications,
   for the same reason.
6. **Read every diff before you run it.** The tests execute the agent's
   code. Read what was written first, and never run a command the agent
   proposes on a checkout that matters. This covers what you run. It does
   not cover the code the agent runs itself while it works, such as the
   tests it runs on its own draft: that code runs before anyone has read
   it, and only the scratch checkout and any isolation limit what it can
   reach.

The profile is a way of working that limits the damage of a mistake. It is
not a security boundary: without further isolation, rules 2 and 3 are
settings of the agent, not limits the machine enforces, and an agent that
leaves them is stopped only by a container or a separate machine with no
credential but the agent's own. Nor does the profile make the code right.

### The review rubric

The provided tests decide whether the claim is supported. The rubric asks
what tests cannot, in this order.

1. **The diff.** Was only the requested file written? Does it import only
   what the specification allows? A solution that imports the reference
   solution passes every test and has shown nothing.
2. **Assumptions.** Which decisions did the agent make that the
   specification left open, and are they acceptable? Ask the agent to list
   them; then look for the ones it did not list.
3. **Units.** Does every term of the acceleration have the unit of an
   acceleration? Is the frequency used as an angular frequency?
4. **Update order.** Is the force evaluated at each stage of the step, at
   that stage's time, position, and velocity? Is the clock the state's?
5. **Tests.** Did the provided tests run unchanged, and what do they not
   cover? An agent's own added tests count for nothing until you have read
   them.
6. **Failure modes.** What does the code do with a step too large, a
   negative mass, a start at another time than zero?

The rubric is the contract's last sentence made into a list: the checks
find that something is wrong, the reading finds what.

### A submission, verified

The page cannot show an agent's code as verified, so it verifies a stand-in
the build can run: one of the faulty simulations above, handed in as if it
were a submission. The report is generated from the findings, in the form
of the contract.

```{python}
#| echo: false
excerpt(experiment.report_on_a_submission)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
print(result.output("submission-report"), end="")
```

The verdict needs no judgement, and the last two lines say what a passing
report would still leave open. A learner's own submission gets the same
report from the same function.

### One recorded session

The session below is an example, not a result. The build did not run it and
cannot check it; it is here to show what the workflow looks like and what a
review adds to passing tests.

::: {.not-verified}
**Example transcript, condensed by the author of this lesson.**
Agent: Claude Fable 5.2 (`claude-fable-5-2`), run as a subagent through the
Claude Agent SDK. Date: 2026-11-18. The sandbox profile was given to the
agent as instructions; the harness of that session did not enforce it.

```text
TASK      The specification of this page, a scratch directory holding it
          and the provided test file, and the profile: write driven.py
          only; run only the tests, the formatter, and the linter; no
          network; do not open the reference solution or the checks;
          at most 12 tool calls and 3 runs of the tests.

AGENT     Read the specification, the test file, and the State and
          Trajectory classes it may import. Wrote driven.py: the classical
          Runge-Kutta method by hand on x' = v,
          v' = (F0 cos(Omega t) - b v - k x) / m, with the time of each
          step computed as t0 + i dt.

TESTS     Run 1: "4 passed". The linter then reported an unsorted import
          block; the agent removed one blank line. Run 2: "4 passed".

AGENT     Reported assumptions the specification did not state: a negative
          number of steps raises an error; zero steps return one row; force
          and omega are not validated; values that are not finite are not
          checked. Reported what the tests do not cover: the refusal of
          invalid inputs; stiff parameters, where the method diverges
          without warning. Reported 11 tool calls and 2 test runs used.

REVIEW    Diff: one new file; imports numpy and the two allowed classes;
          the repository was unchanged after the session.
          Tests, run again by the reviewer: all four checks pass, fitted
          order 4.01.
          Units and update order, by reading: the drive is divided by the
          mass; the force is evaluated at each stage, at that stage's time.
          Not covered by the tests: the four refusals of the interface.
          Checked by hand: each raises the error the specification asks
          for. A start at a time other than zero keeps its clock.
```
:::

The passing tests are the smallest part of the record. The review item with
content is the fifth: the provided tests never call the function with a
negative mass, the agent said so, and the reviewer checked those four cases
by hand. Another session, with another agent or the same one, will differ
in its path and may fail; nothing here says how often an agent succeeds.

What reaches a repository from such a session is a matter of the ordinary
route: a pull request, read by a person, checked by the same tests, and
marked as drafted with an agent. The transcript is never an input of a
build.

## Exercises

::: {.exercise}
**A tolerance that is too loose.** The convergence test accepts a fitted order
within 0.4 of the claim. Compute the fitted orders of velocity Verlet and of
Verlet without the half, and judge each against the claim of order 2 with a
margin of 0.4 and with a margin of 1.5. What does the loose margin do, and what
does that say about choosing a tolerance after seeing the faulty result?

::: {.solution}
```{python}
#| echo: false
excerpt(experiment.margins)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
print(result.output("margins"), end="")
```

A margin of 1.5 passes both: the fault has made the method first order, and
the distance from order 2 is smaller than the margin. The margin has to be
chosen from the scatter of a correct method, here a few hundredths, before the
faulty one is seen; fixed that way, it fails the fault with room to spare.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
**A fault of your own.** Write a stepper that is velocity Verlet except that
the velocity update uses the acceleration at the start of the step only, and
claim order 2 with a bounded energy for it. Predict which tests fail, then run
`verify`.

::: {.solution}
```{python}
#| echo: false
excerpt(experiment.verlet_with_one_acceleration)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
excerpt(experiment.one_acceleration)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
print(result.output("one-acceleration"), end="")
```

The velocity is updated as in explicit Euler, so the method is of order 1
and the convergence test fails. The clock and purity tests pass, and so does
the limit test, which only needs a velocity update that is exact for a
constant force, as this one is. The energy test fails as well, with a band
that grows by many orders of magnitude over the run: a method that is
second order in the position and first order in the velocity is not a
symplectic method of any order. The three failures are one fault seen three
ways, which is the pattern a verifier reads. The linear oscillator would not
show a fault that only matters for a force that depends on the velocity; a
test on the throw with drag of the earlier lessons would be the next one to
add.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
**Drive a coding agent yourself (optional, on your machine).** Give a
coding agent of your choice the specification of the driven oscillator and
the provided tests, under the sandbox profile, with a budget you set
first. Then review its work with the rubric before you believe the tests.
The site does not run this exercise, names no agent as a requirement, and
does not promise that an agent succeeds.

::: {.not-verified}
```bash
# needs: an account with the coding agent's provider, and its credential in
# your environment (see the agent's own documentation)
git clone https://github.com/taspinar/physics-by-construction.git scratch
cd scratch
uv sync --locked
mkdir exercise
# put the specification and the provided test of
# docs/coding-agent-workflow.md into exercise/, start your coding agent
# there with the allowlist and the budget of the profile, and when it is
# done, read the diff; only then:
cd exercise
uv run --locked python -m pytest test_driven.py
```
:::

::: {.solution}
There is no number to compare with: the outcome is the report and your
review. If the four tests pass, the claim of order four is supported on the
oscillator of the checks, and the rubric decides what else you know. Go
through it with the file open. The questions that most often have an answer
are the first, the second, and the fifth: whether the file imports the
reference solution, which assumptions were made silently, and what the
tests do not call. If a test fails, the name of the check and its evidence
say where to look, as in the table of the faulty simulations: a failure of
`units` alone names the unit, a failure of `convergence-order` alone with
every limit passing points at the stages of the step. If the budget ends
first, the session has ended without a result, which is an outcome and not
a reason to raise the budget until the tests pass.
:::
:::
